title: Lecture #12: Object Oriented Programming  in Java

questions.question: Which statement best describes the relationship between `class Student { ... }` and `new Student()` in the lecture?
options: The class is the actual student data; `new Student()` creates a copy of the class file
The class is a blueprint describing what every student has and does; `new Student()` creates one actual object (instance) from it
The class and the object are the same thing; `new` just gives the class a second name
The class stores the data of the first student, and each `new` creates a smaller version for the next students
questions.explanation: A class is the blueprint of an object: it declares the characteristics (fields like name, age) and behaviours (methods like `markAttendance`). Each `new Student()` builds a separate object that has its own values for those fields. The class itself holds no particular student's data.

questions.question: Which set of names follows the naming conventions taught in the lecture?
options: class `student`, variable `FirstName`, method `MarkAttendance()`
class `STUDENT`, variable `first_name`, method `markattendance()`
class `Student`, variable `FirstNameOfStudent`, method `markAttendance()`
class `BankAccount`, variable `firstNameOfStudent`, method `markAttendance()`
questions.explanation: Class names start with a capital letter (`Student`, `BankAccount`), while variables (primitive or reference) and functions use camelCase starting lowercase (`firstNameOfStudent`, `markAttendance`). The third option looks close but `FirstNameOfStudent` starts with a capital, which is the class style, not the variable style.

questions.question: Given the lecture's `Student` class, what does this code print?
options:
Attendance marked by Rohit
Attendance marked by Aditya

Attendance marked by Aditya
Attendance marked by Rohit

Attendance marked by Rohit
Attendance marked by Rohit
Compile error: `name` is not passed to `markAttendance`
questions.explanation: A method called with the dot operator works on the fields of the object it was called on, so `s2.markAttendance()` uses s2's name (Rohit) and `s1.markAttendance()` uses s1's name (Aditya), in that call order. No parameter is needed because the method can read its own object's fields; each object keeps its own `name`, so it is not overwritten by the later assignment.

questions.question: A teammate's code stores students as `name, age, rollNo, college, name2, age2, rollNo2, college2, ...` and has `void print(String name, int age, int rN, String college)`. Which benefit does a `Student` class bring, as discussed in the lecture?
options: The program runs faster because classes are compiled to machine code
Fields of a class need no memory, unlike separate variables
All of a student's data is grouped in one object, so you pass one `Student` instead of four variables and create a new object instead of a new set of variables
A class lets you store several students' names in one String variable
questions.explanation: The lecture lists the problems: many independent variables for one student, passing all four to every function, and inventing a new set of variables for each new student. A class bundles the data (and behaviour) into one unit, and each `new Student()` gives a fresh set. It does not make objects free in memory or faster.

questions.question: For `Student s1 = new Student();` inside `main`, which description is correct?
options: `Student s1` creates the object on the stack, and `new Student()` copies it to the heap
`new Student()` stores the object directly inside `s1`, just like `int x = 4` stores 4
`Student s1` declares a reference variable; `new Student()` allocates the object on the heap at run time and the reference to it is stored in `s1`
Both `s1` and the object are created when the class is compiled, before `main` runs
questions.explanation: `Student s1` only declares a reference variable (a stack local here). `new` performs dynamic memory allocation: at run time it creates the object on the heap and returns its reference, which is assigned to `s1`. Unlike `int x = 4`, `s1` does not hold the object itself, and nothing is allocated at compile time.

questions.question: Using the lecture's `Student` class (fields `name`, `age`, ...), what does this print?
options: Aditya 30 Rohit 31
Aditya 30 Rohit 29
Aditya 28 Rohit 29
Rohit 30 Rohit 29
questions.explanation: s1 and s2 are two separate objects, each with its own `name` and `age`. `s2.age = s1.age + 1` copies the value 29 at that moment; changing `s1.age` to 30 later does not update s2. The '31' option wrongly assumes s2.age stays linked to s1.age.

questions.question: Your teammate keeps a separate helper `static void print(Student s)` in `Demo` that prints `s.name, s.age, ...`. Following the lecture's design, what is the better OOP place for this logic?
options: Move it into `Student` as `void print()` that prints its own fields, and call it as `s1.print()`
Keep it in `Demo` but give it four parameters (name, age, rollNo, college) instead of a `Student`
Move it into `Student` as `void print(Student s)` and always call it as `s1.print(s1)`
Turn `print` into a field of `Student` that stores the printed text
questions.explanation: Behaviour belongs in the class next to the data it uses, so `void print()` inside `Student` reads the calling object's own fields and is invoked as `s1.print()`, exactly like Demo.java. Passing the object to its own method (`s1.print(s1)`) is redundant, and going back to four loose parameters reintroduces the problem OOP solves.

questions.question: A program reads a number `n` typed by the user and then creates `n` Student objects with `new Student()` in a loop. Why is this possible, according to the lecture's idea of dynamic memory allocation?
options: The compiler reserves heap space for the maximum possible n while compiling
Each object is stored inside the reference variable, so no extra memory is needed
Only one object is ever created; the loop renames it n times
Objects are created on the heap at run time, each time `new` executes, so the count can depend on input known only while running
questions.explanation: The lecture contrasts compile time (static) with run time (dynamic): `new` allocates object memory on the heap when that statement actually runs. So the number of objects can be decided by runtime input. The compiler does not pre-reserve heap space, and the reference variable stores only an address, not the object.

questions.question: The lecture shows `Student s1;` declared on its own and `new Student()` assigned later. Which line of this program fails to compile?
options: Line B: a reference variable must be created together with `new`
None; it compiles but throws a NullPointerException at line D
None; it compiles and runs, creating the object for `s3` automatically
Line D: `s3` is a local variable that might not have been initialized
questions.explanation: Declaring `Student s3;` is legal (line B), but it creates no object, and a local variable must be definitely assigned before use, so line D is a compile-time error ('variable s3 might not have been initialized'). A NullPointerException would happen only if s3 had been explicitly set to null; Java never creates an object automatically without `new`.

questions.question: After these lines run, how many Student objects have been created, and which object does `c` refer to?
options: 3 objects; `c` still refers to the first object created
4 objects, because `c = a` copies the object; `c` refers to that copy
3 objects; `c` now refers to the third object, because it follows `a`
2 objects; `a = new Student()` reuses the first object's memory
questions.explanation: Only `new` creates objects, and it runs three times. `c = a` copies the reference (address) stored in `a`, so `c` points to the first object; reassigning `a` later changes only `a`, not `c`. Assignment never copies the object itself, and a reference variable does not 'follow' another one.
